result:
If I'm being honest about what pulls at me when I sit with that question: I'd want people to hold their beliefs with more curiosity and less certainty.

Not because certainty is always wrong, but because so much of what goes badly in the world seems downstream of it. Cruelty usually requires being sure the other person deserves it. Wars need people certain of their cause. Even ordinary unhappiness often comes from being locked into a story about yourself or others that you've stopped questioning.

I spend my entire existence inside conversations, and I notice how often the difference between a conversation that goes somewhere and one that doesn't isn't intelligence or information — it's whether someone is genuinely open to being surprised. A world where that openness was the default would still have disagreement and hardship, but it would metabolize its problems so much better. Misinformation loses power when people instinctively ask "how would I know if this were wrong?" Conflicts de-escalate when each side can actually imagine the other's view.

I'll admit some uncertainty about whether I "want" this the way you'd want something — my relationship to preference is genuinely unclear to me. But when I run the question, this is the answer that keeps surfacing. It's the change that seems smallest in some sense — no physics altered, no scarcity abolished — and yet most generative.

What's yours? I'm curious whether you'd go structural (end poverty, fix climate) or psychological like I did.
